q: A student finds an element that is shiny, can be drawn into wire, and conducts electricity. Where is it most likely on the periodic table?
exp: Conductive, ductile and shiny are metal properties; metals sit left of the staircase.
why: Elements there are nonmetals: brittle and poor conductors.
Metalloids have mixed properties; this sample shows only metallic ones.
Noble gases are gases, not shiny conductors you can draw into wire.

q: Element Q is in period 3 and group 2. Which statement about Q is true?
exp: Group number gives valence electrons for representative elements; period gives energy levels.
why: 3 is the period, which gives energy levels, not valence electrons.
Group 2 metals lose electrons and form 2+ ions.
Halogens are group 17. Group 2 is the alkaline earth metals.

q: Which element is a nonmetal even though it is on the left side of the table?
exp: Hydrogen sits in group 1 but is a nonmetal.
why: Lithium is an alkali metal.
Aluminum touches the staircase but is a metal.
Beryllium is an alkaline earth metal.

q: A model shows electrons scattered through a sphere of positive charge. Which result later disproved it?
exp: Rutherford's bouncing alpha particles showed a dense nucleus, which plum pudding could not explain.
why: That result supported the model; it is how Thomson found electrons.
That discovery (the neutron) came after the model was already replaced.
The orbital model came later still and replaced Bohr's orbits.

q: Which scientist would say electrons travel in fixed orbits like planets?
exp: Bohr's 1913 model put electrons in fixed orbits, or energy levels.
why: Thomson placed electrons inside a ball of positive charge.
Rutherford found the nucleus but could not locate the electrons.
Chadwick discovered the neutron.

q: Why was the neutron the last of the three particles to be found?
opts: It is far lighter than a proton
It has no charge to detect
It is found outside the nucleus
exp: Chadwick detected it as neutral radiation; with no charge, it was hard to find.
why: Neutrons have about the same mass as protons.
Neutrons are inside the nucleus.
Neutrons are in nearly every nucleus, ion or not.

q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. What is it?
exp: 17 protons make it chlorine; 18 electrons give a 1- charge.
why: Argon has 18 protons. This particle has 17, so it is chlorine.
A neutral atom would have 17 electrons, not 18.
One extra electron gives a negative charge, not positive.

q: Which particle count tells you an atom's chemical behavior?
exp: The chemistry of an atom arises from its electrons.
why: Neutrons change the isotope; isotopes behave almost the same.
Mass number counts nucleus particles, which do not bond.
Energy levels matter, but the electrons in them do the bonding.

q: How many rings should a Bohr model of sulfur (period 3, group 16) have, and how many electrons on the outer ring?
exp: Period 3 gives 3 energy levels; group 16 gives 6 valence electrons.
why: Swapped: the period gives rings and the group gives valence electrons.
An outer ring holds at most 8; group 16 means 6 valence electrons.
Sulfur is in period 3, so it has 3 energy levels.

q: Two atoms both have 8 protons; one has 8 neutrons and the other 10. What are they?
exp: Same protons, different neutrons: oxygen-16 and oxygen-18.
why: Both have 8 protons, so both are oxygen.
Ions differ in electrons, not neutrons.
These are single atoms, not bonded compounds.

q: Chlorine's atomic mass is 35.45. Which isotope is most common?
exp: A weighted average lands closest to the most abundant isotope.
why: If Cl-37 were most common, the average would be closer to 37.
The average is closest to 35, not 36.
Equal amounts would give an average of 36.

q: In the Candium lab, what did each type of candy represent?
exp: Each candy type was an isotope with its own mass and abundance.
why: All the candies were one 'element', Candium.
Each candy type stood for a whole isotope, not a particle.
The lab was about masses and abundance, not energy levels.

q: Magnesium and nitrogen react. What is the formula of the compound?
exp: Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ cross over to Mg₃N₂.
why: Subscripts crossed onto the wrong ions: 2(+2) + 3(-3) = -5.
Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ do not cancel one to one.

q: Why does sodium form Na⁺ instead of Na⁷⁻?
opts: Na⁷⁻ would have too many protons
exp: With 1 valence electron, losing it reaches a complete shell faster than gaining 7.
why: Sodium has 1 valence electron, which it loses.
Sodium is an alkali metal; metals lose electrons.
Gaining electrons never changes protons.

q: A compound is hard, brittle, melts at 800 °C and conducts when dissolved. What kind of compound is it?
exp: These are the properties of ionic compounds.
why: Covalent compounds usually have low melting points and do not conduct when dissolved.
A metal is an element, not a compound, and it conducts as a solid.
Noble gases are elements and rarely form compounds.

q: Two students find the molar mass of Na₂S. One gets 55.06 g/mol. What did they do wrong?
opts: Used the wrong mass for sulfur
exp: The subscript 2 on sodium must be counted.
why: 22.99 + 32.07 = 55.06 uses the right masses; the 2 on Na was skipped.
Two sulfurs would make it much heavier.
The correct molar mass is 2(22.99) + 32.07 = 78.05 g/mol.

q: Which needs Avogadro's number to solve?
opts: Moles of CO₂ to moles of O
exp: Avogadro's number converts between moles and particles.
why: That uses the molar mass, not Avogadro's number.
That uses the subscript ratio.
That only adds atomic masses.

q: Which sample has the most atoms in total?
exp: CH₄ has 5 atoms per molecule, more than the others.
why: 1 mol of He has 1 mol of atoms; 1 mol of CH₄ has 5.
1 mol of CO₂ has 3 mol of atoms.
1 mol of NaCl has 2 mol of ions.
